title: Scope and Sequence
text:
How This Course Is Organized
This is a spiral course, not a sequence of topic units. Students do not spend weeks on output, then weeks on input, then weeks on decisions. From the first week, they read real programs that already use output, input, variables, decisions, loops, strings, and lists. Each module comes back to all of these ideas at a deeper level.

Modules are built around themes and anchor programs, not single programming constructs. Each module has a purpose students can see (find out about this computer, check whether it meets a need, measure how fast it is, keep passwords safe, troubleshoot the network, investigate data).
Reading makes early depth possible. Students can read and predict code that uses a loop or a list weeks before they are asked to write one. When code uses something not yet taught, the teacher explains it briefly and moves on: “You’ll learn to write these properly later.”
Each idea moves through four levels across the course: read it, modify it, write it, then design with it.
Not project-based. Lessons stay teacher-led and structured (see the teaching approach); a full independent project comes only at the end.

title: Scope and Sequence
text:
Practising the Basics
A spiral brings every idea back, but basics also need practice until they’re automatic. Each module has:

A Skill Builder page: short drills on the module’s basics and earlier ones (predict the output, fix the error, Parsons problems, fill in the blank, write a tiny program). Drills can be plainer than lessons; not every exercise needs to be about hardware.
Quick Builds: two small graded programs before the module assignment, such as a system banner and a parts receipt in Module 1, or a file name cleaner in Module 4. Each is the Make product of a named lesson, so it costs no extra class time.
A work period: in Modules 1–6, the period before the test is a short review followed by class time for the module assignment.
Spaced warm-ups: every lesson’s review includes a question from two or more lessons back, often an earlier module.

Course Tools

Sample folder generator (planned): make_sample_folder.py builds a realistic, messy folder for file lessons: text, CSV, Python, and log files, real PNG images, zip archives, sub-folders, awkward names, duplicates, and backdated files. It uses only the standard library. With a fixed seed every student gets the same folder, so answer keys have exact answers; --seed gives each student a different one. It deletes only inside folders it created itself, so students can rebuild after a mistake. An optional --download adds real, licence-checked files hosted on this site, falling back to local generation if the network blocks it. Used in Modules 1, 5 (reading its download code), 6, and 7.

title: Scope and Sequence
text:
Modules
Each module’s overview page has its planned lessons, anchor programs, and assignment. This section is the summary.

Module 1 — About This Computer (15 h)
Purpose: Ask the computer about itself.
Anchor programs: a two-line program that prints the CPU type (platform.machine()); a labelled computer report built from the platform module and stored in variables; a greeter that asks the user’s name and gives a hardware summary; a report that loops through a list of facts.
Pacing: one library first. Lessons 1–2 use only platform, starting from a single line. Other modules (os for cores, shutil for storage) wait until Module 2.

Taught explicitly: what a program is; reading and predicting output; import and calling a module’s functions; print() in depth (arguments, sep, end, escape characters) and f-strings; variables and the basic types (str, int, float); simple arithmetic; tracing line by line; finding tools with dir() and the documentation; comments and naming conventions; syntax and run-time errors and how to read them
Met through reading: input(), a simple if, a for loop over a list
Computer science: CPU types and operating systems; where code runs (classroom computer, browser, cloud); where variables live (RAM) and where arithmetic happens (CPU); source code vs. machine code (bytecode with dis); interpreters vs. compilers; applications, languages, and operating systems; organizing program files

Quick Builds: System Banner, Parts Receipt. Assignment: Computer Report Card. Expectations: A1.1, A2.1, A2.2, A3.1, A4.2, A4.3, A4.4, C1.1, C1.4, C2.1, C3.1, C3.3, C3.4, C3.5


Module 2 — Spec Checker (15 h)
Purpose: Decide whether a computer meets a user’s needs.
Anchor programs: a core counter (os.cpu_count()); a storage calculator (why “1 TB” shows as 931 GB); a drive gauge (shutil.disk_usage()); “Will this game run?”; a monitor sharpness (pixels per inch) calculator.

Taught explicitly: input and type conversion; data types; arithmetic, integer division, remainder, order of operations; comparison and logical operators; if/elif/else; try/except for bad input; user-friendly prompts and messages; test plans with normal, boundary, and invalid cases
Met through modifying: a loop over a list of requirements; .strip() and .lower() for cleaning input
Computer science: internal components, specifications, and peripherals related to user needs; the input-process-output model

Quick Builds: Storage Unit Converter, Battery Life Estimator. Assignment: Will It Run? Expectations: A1.1, A1.3, A1.4, A2.1, A2.2, A4.1, A4.3, A4.5, B1.1, B1.3, B2.5, B3.2, B3.3, B4.4, C1.1, C1.2, C1.3


Module 3 — Benchmark Lab (14 h)
Purpose: Measure how fast the computer really is.
Anchor programs: count to a million with a stopwatch; a benchmark suite (counting, string building, checking primes); a study timer; a reaction timer; “Is shuffle really random?”; a typing speed test.

Taught explicitly: for loops and range(); while loops; counters and accumulators; nested loops and decisions; the time and random modules; reading and modifying first functions; flow charts and pseudocode; program skeletons; debugging by tracing and printing variables
Met through modifying: a list of counts; random.shuffle(); strings in prompts and messages
Computer science: benchmarks and fair tests; how CPU type, cores, and the interpreter affect speed; running the same code on different machines; determining primes

Quick Builds: Download Time Table, Study Timer. Assignment: Typing Speed Test, with a benchmark report. Expectations: A2.2, A2.3, A3.1, A3.2, A4.1, A4.4, B1.1, B2.1, B2.4, B3.2, B4.5, C1.2, C1.4


Module 4 — Passwords and Secret Messages (15 h)
Purpose: Learn how computers store text, and keep it safe.
Anchor programs: a binary and hex converter; a Unicode inspector; a password strength checker; a crack-time estimator (using Module 3’s benchmark); a Caesar cipher (short activity) that shows why simple ciphers aren’t secure.

Taught explicitly: strings as sequences (indexing, slicing, traversal, methods); ord() and chr(); writing functions with parameters and return values; local and global scope; reusable modules; secrets and hashlib
Computer science: binary, hexadecimal, ASCII, and Unicode; how websites store passwords; cryptography as a research area; malware and a system protection plan

Quick Builds: Username Maker, File Name Cleaner. Assignment: Password Toolkit, with a home system protection plan. Expectations: A1.2, A3.1, A3.2, A4.1, B1.1, B2.3, B4.4, C2.2, D2.1


Module 5 — On the Network (14 h)
Purpose: Find out how the computer talks to the rest of the world.
Anchor programs: “Who am I on the network?” (host name and local IP address); an IP address explainer (list of octets in binary, private or public); a website lookup (DNS); a response timer; a download speed test.

Taught explicitly: lists as one-dimensional arrays (elements, indexes, bounds); .split() and .append(); count, total, highest, lowest; exceptions for network failures; testing with good, slow, and broken inputs; writing files (a CSV log with timestamps); socket, ipaddress, urllib, and datetime
Computer science: IP addresses, DNS, ports, packets, and routers; private and public networks; firewalls; running a web server; distributed computing; data flow diagrams

Quick Builds: Speed Log Summary, Web Address Splitter. Assignment: Is It Me or the Wi-Fi? Expectations: A1.2, A1.5, A1.6, A2.3, A3.1, A3.2, A4.5, B1.1, B2.4, B3.3, D2.1


Module 6 — Data Detective (15 h)
Purpose: Investigate data about the computer and its use.
Anchor programs: a folder detective on a generated sample folder (files by type, total size, biggest, oldest, duplicates); a top-ten list of the biggest files kept in sorted order; a backup maker that verifies copies with hashes; an analysis of the students’ own Module 5 network log; the computer lab’s yearly power bill from a CSV file.

Taught explicitly: lists and parallel lists; linear search; highest and lowest value; inserting into a sorted list and deleting from the middle; reading CSV files; breaking a program into functions; structure charts; describing and comparing designs; testing with a full range of cases
Computer science: organizing files and folders; backing up and archiving (the 3-2-1 rule); environmental and health effects of computer use; reducing them; e-waste, refurbishing, and community partners

Quick Builds: Extension Report, Duplicate Finder. Assignment: Folder Detective. Expectations: A1.5, A1.6, A2.3, A3.2, A4.4, A4.5, B2.2, B2.3, B2.4, B3.1, C2.1, C2.3, D1.1, D1.2, D1.3, D1.4


Module 7 — Software Development Project (16 h)
Purpose: Plan, build, test, and present a useful program for a real person.

Part 1, teacher-led class project (about 4 h): “Lab Health Check”, built by teams from earlier modules’ code; the software development life cycle, a Gantt chart, and milestones practised together
Part 2, individual or pair project (about 12 h): a real user; specification by interview or questionnaire; design documents; test plan first; written status reports; presentation
Design level: students choose and combine every idea from the spiral

Expectations: A4.2, A4.5, B1.2, B2.1, B2.2, B2.3, B2.4, B2.5, B4.1, B4.2, B4.3, B4.4, B4.5, B4.6, C3.2


Computer Science in the World (6 h, between Modules 2–6)
Purpose: See where computer science leads.
Five short lessons, each placed after a module and tied to it (careers in hardware after Module 2, distributed computing after Module 3, security after Module 4, collaborative research after Module 5, postsecondary programs after Module 6), plus a research report submitted in stages.
Expectations: D2.1, D2.2, D2.3, D3.1, D3.2, D3.3, D3.4, D3.5

title: Scope and Sequence
text:
Assessment Overview
Following Ontario’s Growing Success policy: 70% of the final grade comes from evaluations during the course and 30% from final evaluations.

Every lesson: an exit ticket, usually a code-reading or tracing question (assessment for and as learning, not counted toward the grade).
Within each module: short quizzes, two Quick Builds (small graded programs), and the module assignment, which adds to the student’s toolkit.
End of Modules 1–6: a module test that always includes a code-reading and tracing section and a short basics section. Because the course spirals, every test may include earlier ideas.
Computer Science in the World: the staged research report.
Final 30%: the Module 7 software development project and a final exam that includes code reading and tracing.

title: Scope and Sequence
text:
Python Notes for Teachers
The 2008 curriculum uses general terms. In Python:

Constants (A1.1) are a naming convention (UPPER_CASE); Python does not enforce them.
One-dimensional arrays (A1.5, A1.6) are taught as Python lists, used with a single data type and fixed purpose.
Procedures (A3.2) are functions that do not return a value.
Compiler error messages (A4.3) appear in Python as tracebacks; C3.4 contrasts Python’s interpreter with compiled languages such as C or Java.
Hardware and network programs use only the standard library (platform, then os, shutil, time, socket, ipaddress, and urllib). Network programs need a real computer: the site’s browser boxes can’t open network connections. Results depend on where the code runs: macOS reports itself as “Darwin”; the course website’s runnable code reports a browser virtual computer (wasm32, Emscripten); Google Colab reports a Google cloud server (typically x86_64, Linux). These differences are a deliberate teaching point. Use platform.machine() for the CPU type; platform.processor() is unreliable across systems. Total RAM is not available from the standard library.

title: Scope and Sequence
text:
Teaching Approach
Every lesson follows the course’s reading-first approach: students read, trace, and predict code before they write it. Each lesson opens with review and a useful problem (“How could we check 500 files without opening each one?”), then moves through a teacher-led worked example, then Predict, Run, Investigate, Modify, and Make (PRIMM). Writing new code from scratch always comes after reading and modifying.

title: Module 6: Data Detective
text:
Planned module. This page shows the direction for Module 6. Lessons, slides, and practice pages are not written yet.
The big idea: students investigate data about their own computer use. They scan a messy folder to find out what’s taking up space, keep a sorted top-ten list of the biggest files, write a backup script that proves its copies are perfect, analyze the network log they collected in Module 5, and use data on power use and e-waste to work out what the computer lab costs to run. Lists and list algorithms (search, highest and lowest, sorted insert and delete) are the core, with functions and structure charts to organize bigger programs.
Why students care: “My computer is full” and “Where did that file go?” are everyday problems. So is losing work with no backup. Students leave with tools they can use on their own computers.
Expectations: A1.5, A1.6, A2.3, A3.2, A4.4, A4.5, B2.2, B2.3, B2.4, B3.1, C2.1, C2.3, D1.1, D1.2, D1.3, D1.4

title: Module 6: Data Detective
text:
Anchor Programs

Folder detective: lists every file in a folder with os.scandir(), counts files by type, totals their size, and finds duplicates by hash. It runs on a sample folder built by the course’s generator script.
Top ten biggest files: keeps a sorted list, inserting each new file in its place and dropping the smallest (add to a sorted array; delete from the middle, B3.1).
Backup maker: copies a project folder into a dated .zip with shutil.make_archive(), checks each copy against the original with a SHA-256 hash (Module 4 again), and writes a backup log.
Network log analyzer: the students’ own Module 5 log: average response by day and time, and the worst hour.
Lab power bill: reads a CSV file of device wattages and calculates the yearly cost and energy use of the computer lab.

title: Module 6: Data Detective

Assignment (Planned): Folder Detective
Students run their folder detective on a sample folder generated with their own seed (so every student’s results are different). The program reports the number of files of each type, the total size, the top ten biggest files, the oldest files, and any duplicates, and suggests what to archive. Running it on their own Downloads folder is an optional extension. Students hand in the program, a structure chart, a test plan, and a short write-up of what they found and what they did about it.
Adds to the toolkit: folder_detective.py and backup.py, which import from the student’s earlier toolkit files.

title: Module 6: Data Detective
text:
Notes for Teachers

Open computers needed. On a managed computer, this module’s problem is files: the course folder and sample folder must stay put between classes (no reset on log-off), and security software may flag a program that reads, hashes, and copies hundreds of files. Check the requirements table with IT before the module starts.
Sample folder, not students’ own files. make_sample_folder.py (planned; see the Scope and Sequence) builds the same messy folder for everyone, or a different one per student with --seed. If a program wrecks it, run the script again.
Read-only programs. Nothing in this module deletes or moves files. Tell students why: programs that delete files are dangerous, and you always back up first. A “dry run” (print what would happen) is the safe habit.
Lists, not dictionaries. The curriculum asks for one-dimensional arrays, so use lists (and parallel lists). Dictionaries can appear as a marked extension.
Electricity rates: use the current Ontario rate, and let students look it up.

title: Module 4: Passwords and Secret Messages
text:
Planned module. This page shows the direction for Module 4. Lessons, slides, and practice pages are not written yet.
The big idea: students learn how computers store text, and how to keep it safe. They start with binary and hexadecimal, discover that every character is a number, then build tools for everyday security: a password strength checker, a password generator, a crack-time estimator, and a Caesar cipher they then learn to break.
Why students care: every student has passwords, and most reuse them. This module shows, with their own programs, why length matters, how websites store passwords, and how to protect a home computer.
Expectations: A1.2, A3.1, A3.2, A4.1, B1.1, B2.3, B4.4, C2.2, D2.1

title: Module 4: Passwords and Secret Messages
text:
Anchor Programs

Binary and hex converter: bin(), hex(), int(text, 2); where hex shows up (colour codes, MAC addresses, error codes).
What’s in a message? Prints the Unicode number of every character, including emoji.
Password strength checker: length, upper and lower case, digits, symbols, and common passwords.
How long to crack? Uses the Module 3 benchmark’s guesses per second to estimate brute-force time.
Caesar cipher (short activity): encode, decode, and break by trying every shift, to show why simple ciphers aren’t secure.

Assignment (Planned): Password Toolkit
Students build password_tools.py, a module of their own functions (strength check, generator, crack-time estimate), and a short program that uses it. They hand in the code, a test plan, and a system protection plan for a real computer at home: what threats it faces and the specific steps (updates, accounts, backups, antivirus, browser habits) that protect it.

title: Module 4: Passwords and Secret Messages
text:
Notes for Teachers

Never ask for real passwords. Use made-up examples throughout, and say so out loud.
Hashing, not encryption. Keep the distinction simple: you can’t get a password back from its hash, so websites compare hashes.
Ethics: cracking is shown only on the student’s own made-up passwords and the class’s Caesar messages. A short discussion of the law and responsible disclosure fits here.

title: Module 2: Spec Checker
text:
Planned module. This page shows the direction for Module 2. Lessons, slides, and practice pages are not written yet.
The big idea: students decide whether a computer meets someone’s needs. They measure the classroom computer (cores, storage, free space), turn raw numbers into sizes people understand, and write programs that answer real questions: Is there room for this download? Will this game run? Which laptop suits this person?
Why students care: every student has stood in a store, or on a website, wondering which computer to buy, or why their “1 TB” drive shows only 931 GB. This module answers those questions with code.
Expectations: A1.1, A1.3, A1.4, A2.1, A2.2, A4.1, A4.3, A4.5, B1.1, B1.3, B2.5, B3.2, B3.3, B4.4, C1.1, C1.2, C1.3

title: Module 2: Spec Checker
text:
Anchor Programs

Core counter: os.cpu_count(), then a report of what the cores mean for multitasking.
Storage calculator: bytes to kilobytes, megabytes, and gigabytes; why manufacturers and operating systems disagree (1000 vs. 1024).
Drive gauge: shutil.disk_usage() reports total, used, and free space, with a percentage and a warning level.
Will This Game Run? compares this computer to a game’s published minimum requirements.
Screen sharpness calculator: pixels per inch from a monitor’s resolution and size (the hypotenuse formula, B3.2).

title: Module 2: Spec Checker
text:
Assignment (Planned): Will It Run?
Students pick a real game or app with published minimum requirements. Their program:

Reads what it can from the computer (operating system, CPU type, cores, free storage).
Asks the user for what Python can’t find (RAM, graphics card).
Reports each requirement as pass or fail, with a clear summary and friendly messages for bad input.

They also hand in a test plan (normal, boundary, and invalid cases) and a one-paragraph recommendation: should this person upgrade, and what?
Adds to the toolkit: drive_check.py: storage and core checks with warning levels, reused by later modules.

title: Getting Output Right
section: Would you hand this to someone?
text:
Would you hand this to someone?
Computer report for LAB-PC-14
CPU type: AMD64
Operating system: Windows

A real system tool (systeminfo on Windows):
Host Name:                 LAB-PC-14
OS Name:                   Microsoft Windows 11 Pro
System Type:               x64-based PC


Open with the problem: “Our Lesson 2 report works, but would you hand it to someone?” Then run the real tool in a terminal: systeminfo (Windows), system_profiler SPSoftwareDataType (macOS), or hostnamectl (Linux / Raspberry Pi). Ask: what makes it easy to read? Labels, labels that line up, blank lines, a title. “Somebody wrote this tool. Underneath, it’s a program printing lines with careful spacing. Today we learn to control every character.”

title: Getting Output Right
text:
Settings inside print()
print("System", "Windows")
print("System", "Windows", sep=": ")


Commas: print() puts one space between things. That’s sep
sep=": " changes it for this line
end changes what comes at the end (normally a new line)



TEACHER PROMPT (first use of keyword arguments): “When we give print() several things separated by commas, it puts one space between them. That space is a setting called sep, short for separator. sep=‘:’ changes the setting for this one line: the name, an equals sign, then the new value, after the things to print. There’s a second setting, end. Normally print() finishes by moving to a new line; end changes what it prints instead. These are keyword arguments: the keyword tells Python which setting we mean.”

title: Getting Output Right
text:
Predict, then step
import platform

system = platform.system()
print("System", system)
print("System", system, sep=": ")
print("Checking", end="... ")
print("done")
print()
print("End of report")

About 10 minutes. Students write the exact output first, showing spaces as dots on the sep and end lines. Ask: Which line prints nothing but still changes the output? Why do lines 6 and 7 end up on one line? After line 6: “end replaced the new line with ‘…’, so the next print carries on from there.” After line 8: “An empty print() prints only its end, a new line. That’s how we make a blank line.”

title: Getting Output Right
text:
Special characters
print("Name:\tLAB-PC-14")
print("System:\tWindows")
print("Computer name:\tLAB-PC-14")
print("Line one\nLine two")

TEACHER PROMPT (first use of escape characters): “means new line. eans tab: jump to the next tab stop. The backslash tells Python the next letter is special; it won’t be printed.” Ask: lines 1 and 2 line up, line 3 doesn’t. Why? Tab stops are every 8 characters, and “Computer name:” is 14 characters long. How many lines does line 4 make?

title: Getting Output Right
text:
Quotes, commas, and plus
import platform

cpu = platform.machine()
print("This computer's CPU is", cpu)
print('The label says "', cpu, '"')
print("CPU:" + cpu)
print("CPU: " + cpu)

Ask: Why doesn’t the apostrophe in line 4 end the string? How does line 5 print double quotes, and why the spaces inside them? What’s different about lines 6 and 7? Challenge: rewrite line 5 with sep=“” so there are no spaces inside the quotes. TEACHER PROMPT: “A comma gives print() separate things, and print() adds the spaces. A plus sign joins two strings into one thing first, with nothing added. If you want a space, you type it.” Keep + with numbers for Lesson 5.

title: Getting Output Right
text:
Spot the problem: A
import platform

print('It's a', platform.system(), 'computer')
print("Done")

TEACHER PROMPT (first syntax error): “Nothing ran, not even line 1. A syntax error means Python couldn’t understand the program at all, so it refused to start. The message points to the line where it got confused.” Fix it two ways: double quotes around the string, or '.

title: Getting Output Right
text:
Spot the problem: B
print("Save your work in C:\temp\new")
print("Done")

“This one ran to the end, and it’s still wrong. That’s a logic error: no message, just the wrong output. You only catch it by predicting what should happen.” nd changed the folder name. Fix with \ (or forward slashes). This matters again in Lesson 6, with paths.

title: About This Course
text:
The Philosophy

1. Read before you write
Students read code before they write it. Every new idea is first met by reading a short program, predicting what it will do, and tracing it line by line. Writing new code comes last, once students can read it fluently. Every worksheet opens with reading tasks, and every quiz and test includes a code-reading section.


2. Start deep, with real code
Because students read first, they can meet real, interesting programs long before they could write them. The first program students see isn’t “Hello, World”. It asks the computer what kind of processor it has. Students don’t need to understand every line on day one. The parts they can’t yet explain become reasons to keep learning.


3. One new idea at a time
Deep doesn’t mean fast. Lessons start small, often from a single line, and add one piece at a time. Module 1 uses only one library until students are comfortable with it.


4. A spiral, not a list of topics
The course isn’t divided into an output unit, then an input unit, then a decisions unit. Students meet output, input, decisions, loops, strings, and lists early, inside programs they read. Each module comes back to these ideas at a deeper level. Each idea moves through four stages over the course: read it, modify it, write it, then design with it. The spiral table shows where each idea sits in each module.


5. Teacher-led, then gradually independent
Lessons use explicit, direct instruction. The teacher models a worked example, thinking aloud, and students then practise with steadily less support. Each lesson follows the PRIMM sequence: students Predict what code will do, Run it, Investigate how it works, Modify it, and finally Make their own. The course builds toward an independent software project at the end, not from one at the start.

title: About This Course
text:
Built on Research
This approach draws on research about how novices learn to program:

Students who can’t reliably read and trace code have trouble writing it (Lister et al., 2004; Lopez et al., 2008).
Novices learn more from explicit instruction and worked examples than from open-ended discovery (Sweller & Cooper, 1985; Kirschner et al., 2006).
Effective lessons review prior learning, present new material in small steps, model, and guide practice before independent work (Rosenshine, 2012).
PRIMM puts reading and predicting ahead of writing in programming lessons (Sentance et al., 2019).

title: Before You Begin
Before You Begin
text:
Student Computers
Students need a place to run, change, break, and fix programs every day, not only to read them. In order of preference:

1. Standalone refurbished computers
The best choice. Older desktops and laptops are cheap, run Python perfectly well, and can be set up with no restrictions, outside the board’s management.

One computer per student for the semester. The student keeps their files on it, and looks after it: installing updates, making backups, and following the protection plan they write in Module 4. Looking after a real computer is part of the course.
Reset at the end of the semester. A fresh install of Linux takes under an hour and gives the next class a clean start.
Network: ask IT about a separate or guest network, so unmanaged computers can reach the internet for Module 5 without being on the board’s own network.
In Canada, the federal Computers for Schools Plus program supplies refurbished computers to schools. In Ontario it’s run by Renewed Computer Technology. Schools can order through Computers for Schools Ontario.
Many older computers can’t run Windows 11, and Windows 10 stopped receiving security updates in October 2025. A free Linux system (for example, Ubuntu or Linux Mint) runs well on older hardware and comes with Python already installed.
A room with a mix of Windows, macOS, and Linux computers is a bonus. Each one gives different answers to the same program, which is exactly what Lesson 1 investigates.
Refurbishing ties into the curriculum: expectation D1.4 names “private companies that refurbish computers” as an example.



2. School computers that IT has opened up
Lab or classroom computers can work if IT can give students what the table above lists: Python and an editor, the terminal, files that persist, and network access from Python. A dedicated “computer science” image, or a separate lab that isn’t reset every night, is the usual solution. Ask before the semester starts, not the week of Lesson 1.


3. Raspberry Pi and other small computers
A Raspberry Pi is a small, inexpensive computer. Raspberry Pi OS comes with Python 3 and Thonny already installed. Each one needs a power supply, a microSD card, and a monitor, keyboard, and mouse (classroom monitors often work). Its ARM processor reports something different again (on the 64-bit system, aarch64 and Linux), which makes for a good comparison. Other small or portable computers that can install Python work too.






NoteStudents’ own computers



We don’t recommend requiring students to bring their own computers. Not every student has one, it raises privacy and school-policy questions, and a mistake in a student’s program could affect their personal files.
Where your school allows it and a student prefers to use their own computer, the course is designed to keep the risk low. File lessons use a generated sample folder, not personal files, and Module 6’s programs only read files, never delete them. Suggest a separate user account for course work.








TipChromebooks



If your board allows it, a Chromebook’s Linux development environment can install Python and Thonny. The code runs inside a Linux container, so it reports Linux rather than ChromeOS. That’s a good discussion point, but it isn’t the same as a computer running Python directly.

title: Lesson 1: Ask the Computer About Itself
section: Teach: Two Lines of Python (15 min)
text:
Teach: Two Lines of Python (15 min)
Show this program and read it aloud before running it.
import platform

print(platform.machine())






TipTeacher prompt



Think aloud while reading, one line at a time:

“import platform brings in a module: a toolbox of ready-made code that comes with Python. This one can answer questions about the computer.”
“platform.machine() asks one question: what type of CPU is this? The dot means ‘the machine tool from the platform toolbox’. The parentheses mean ‘use it now’.”
“print() shows the answer on the screen.”
“Python runs a program from top to bottom, one line at a time.”



Now run it on the classroom computer (Thonny, IDLE, or VS Code). Compare the answer with the warm-up guesses.
What the answer means. The CPU type names the family of processor and the instructions it understands:








Answer
Meaning
Found in




arm64 or aarch64
64-bit ARM processor
Apple silicon Macs, most phones and tablets, some Chromebooks and Windows laptops


x86_64 or AMD64
64-bit Intel or AMD processor
Most Windows laptops and desktops, older Macs, most servers



Windows reports Intel and AMD processors as AMD64 because AMD designed the 64-bit version of this processor family.

text:
Predict, Then Run (15 min)
Read this program without running it, then answer (students write in their tracing notebooks):

Which words will appear exactly as they are written in the code?
Which parts will depend on the computer?

Type your prediction in the box. Then press Step to run the program one line at a time, and compare each line of output with your prediction.






TipTeacher prompt: the step-through box (first use)



Before anyone presses Step, explain the colours:

“This box runs the program one line at a time. Nothing has run yet.”
“The red arrow on a yellow line marks the next line Python will run. It hasn’t run yet.”
“When I press Step, that line runs and turns green. Green means just ran. The arrow moves to the next line.”
“Anything the program prints appears in the Output box the moment its line turns green. Your prediction stays above it, so you can compare.”
“Back replays a step. Run all jumps to the end. Start over resets everything.”

Then: “Write your prediction first. No pressing Step until you’ve committed.”


import platform

print("CPU type:", platform.machine())
print("Operating system:", platform.system())
print("Computer name:", platform.node())
Now run the same program on the classroom computer (Thonny, IDLE, or VS Code). Which lines of output are the same as on this page? Which are different?

title: Lesson 1: Ask the Computer About Itself
text:
Teacher Notes

Why platform only. Every platform function follows one pattern (platform.something() gives back text), is safe to experiment with, and answers a question students care about. Other modules (os for cores, shutil for storage) come later, one at a time.
machine(), not processor(). platform.processor() is unreliable: it returns a long description on Windows, arm on Apple silicon, and often nothing on Linux or in the browser.
Three places, three computers.

Classroom computer: the real hardware, e.g. arm64 / Darwin (macOS) or AMD64 / Windows. macOS reports itself as “Darwin”, the name of its core.
This web page: Python runs inside the browser (Pyodide, WebAssembly). It reports wasm32, Emscripten, and emscripten: a small virtual computer that exists only inside the browser tab, though it still uses the classroom computer’s processor underneath.
Google Colab: the code runs on a Google server in a data centre. It typically reports x86_64, Linux, and a random-looking machine name. Check by running the program in Colab before class.

Colab access. Many school boards disable Colab for student accounts, so plan it as a teacher demonstration. For setting up classroom computers, see Before You Begin.
Predict, then run. The step-through box keeps the prediction next to the real output. Encourage students to commit to a prediction before pressing Step; the Back button lets them replay any line.
First load. The step-through box and the runnable boxes download Python into the browser the first time (about 10 MB), which can take a few seconds.
Slides. Open the slides on the projector and this plan on your own screen. Press S in the slides to open speaker view, which shows the teacher prompts and timings.
Spiral. Students meet import, function calls, and comma-separated print() items through reading today. Variables come in Lesson 2.

section: Teach: What Else Is in the Toolbox? (15 min)

Teach: What Else Is in the Toolbox? (15 min)
Open with the problem: “Lesson 1 asked platform three questions. What else does it know about this computer? And how do we make a program remember an answer instead of asking twice?”
A module can contain many tools. dir() lists them. Run it and read the list together.












TipTeacher prompt



Think aloud while reading the list:

“Names starting with an underscore, like _comparable_version, are for Python’s own use. We skip those.”
“Some names look familiar from Lesson 1: machine, system, node, python_version, release.”
“Others are new: platform, architecture, version, uname. The name gives a hint, but the documentation tells us for sure.”

system = platform.system()

TipTeacher prompt: reading an error (first use)

“The message under the buttons has three parts: the line number, the kind of error (AttributeError), and a description in plain words. Read them in that order.”
“Errors aren’t failures. They’re Python telling us exactly where to look.”

Variables. A variable is a name that stores a value. cpu = platform.machine() asks the question once and keeps the answer, so the program can use it later, as many times as needed.
Step-through box. It runs the real program in the browser, so platform works and the variables hold the browser’s answers ('wasm32', 'Emscripten'). Python Tutor is not used here because it does not allow the platform module.
Changing a variable. Introduced briefly, through reading only: a variable holds one value at a time, and a new value replaces the old one. Students trace it again in the practice and in Assignment Part A. Updating a variable from its own value (count = count + 1) comes later, when programs start calculating.
dir() output is long and includes names starting with _; tell students to skip those. In the browser and on the classroom computer, the lists may differ slightly between Python versions.
Spot the problem. Without parentheses, platform.machine is the tool itself, not its answer, so Python prints a description of the function, e.g. <function machine at 0x104cb3e20>. The AttributeError says the module has no tool by that name. The step-through box highlights the line that caused the error and shows the error type and message; Thonny, IDLE, and VS Code show the same information as a full traceback, which students should learn to read too.
Slides. Open the slides on the projector and this plan on your own screen. Press S in the slides for speaker view.
Spiral. Students now write variables and read error messages. Calculating with values (os.cpu_count(), storage in gigabytes) comes in Module 2.

At a Glance

Big idea: a real system tool is mostly careful output. print() has settings (sep and end) and special characters (\n, \t) that control exactly what appears on the screen.
Students will: compare their Lesson 2 report with the output of a real system tool, predict output character by character, and find two mistakes: one that crashes and one that doesn’t.
Students make: the System Banner Quick Build, a boxed title banner with the computer’s facts underneath (started in class, finished for next class).

After class: Lesson 3 practice and the System Banner Quick Build.
Where it fits: builds on Lesson 2’s report. Lesson 4 uses f-strings to put the computer’s answers inside the banner’s box, lined up.

section: Teach: What Makes Output Readable? (15 min)
text:
Teach: What Makes Output Readable? (15 min)
Open with the problem: “Our Lesson 2 report works, but would you hand it to someone? Here’s what a real system tool prints.”
On your demonstration computer, open a terminal and run the tool for your operating system:








Operating system
Command
What it shows




Windows
systeminfo
Host name, OS name and version, processor, memory


macOS
system_profiler SPSoftwareDataType
macOS version, computer name, time since start-up


Linux or Raspberry Pi
hostnamectl
Host name, operating system, kernel, architecture



A few lines of systeminfo look like this:
Host Name:                 LAB-PC-14
OS Name:                   Microsoft Windows 11 Pro
System Type:               x64-based PC
Ask: “What makes this easy to read?” Collect answers: a label on every line, labels that line up, blank lines between groups, a title. Then: “Somebody wrote this tool. Underneath, it’s a program printing lines with careful spacing. Today we learn to control every character.”
Then show how print() handles several things at once:
print("System", "Windows")
print("System", "Windows", sep=": ")






TipTeacher prompt: settings inside print() (first use)




“When we give print() several things separated by commas, it puts one space between them. That space is a setting called sep, short for separator.”
“sep=": " changes the setting for this one line. The name, an equals sign, then the new value. It goes after the things to print.”
“There’s a second setting, end. Normally print() finishes by moving to a new line. end changes what it prints at the end instead.”
“These are called keyword arguments: the keyword tells Python which setting we mean. Other Python tools have them too.”

title: Lesson 3: Getting Output Right
text:
Predict, Then Step (10 min)
Read this program without running it, then answer in tracing notebooks:

Write the exact output, one line per row. Show every space as a dot (·) on the lines that use sep and end.
Which line prints nothing but still changes the output?
Lines 6 and 7 are two print() calls. Why does their output end up on one line?

Type your prediction in the box, then press Step.
import platform

system = platform.system()
print("System", system)
print("System", system, sep=": ")
print("Checking", end="... ")
print("done")
print()
print("End of report")






TipTeacher prompt



After line 6 runs: “Look at the output box. The line isn’t finished: end replaced the new line with ..., so the next print() carries on from there.” After line 8: “An empty print() prints only its end, which is a new line. That’s how we make a blank line.”

title: Lesson 3: Getting Output Right
text:
Investigate (20 min)

Special characters (5 min)
A backslash inside a string starts an escape sequence: two characters that stand for one special character.






TipTeacher prompt: escape characters (first use)




“\n means new line. \t means tab: jump to the next tab stop, like the Tab key in a word processor.”
“The backslash tells Python that the next letter is special. It won’t be printed.”



print("Name:\tLAB-PC-14")
print("System:\tWindows")
print("Computer name:\tLAB-PC-14")
print("Line one\nLine two")

Lines 1 and 2 line up. Line 3 doesn’t. Why? (Hint: tab stops are every 8 characters. Count the characters in Computer name:.)
How many lines of output does line 4 make?



Quotes, commas, and plus (10 min)
import platform

cpu = platform.machine()
print("This computer's CPU is", cpu)
print('The label says "', cpu, '"')
print("CPU:" + cpu)
print("CPU: " + cpu)

Line 4’s text has an apostrophe in it. Why doesn’t that end the string early?
Line 5 prints double quotation marks. How? Why are there spaces inside them in the output?
Lines 6 and 7 join text with + instead of a comma. What’s different about the output? Which version would you put in a report?
Rewrite line 5 so the output is The label says "wasm32", with no spaces inside the quotation marks. (Hint: sep.)







TipTeacher prompt



“A comma gives print() separate things, and print() adds the spaces. A plus sign joins two strings into one thing first, with nothing added. If you want a space, you type it.” Leave + with numbers for Lesson 5: “+ only joins text to text. We’ll see what happens with numbers soon.”




Spot the problem (5 min)
Both programs have a mistake. Predict what will happen, then step through each.
Program A
import platform

print('It's a', platform.system(), 'computer')
print("Done")
Program B
print("Save your work in C:\temp\new")
print("Done")






TipTeacher prompt: a syntax error (first use)



After Program A: “Nothing ran. Not even line 1. A syntax error means Python couldn’t understand the program at all, so it refused to start. The message points to the line where it got confused.”
After Program B: “This one ran to the end, and it’s still wrong. That’s a logic error: no message, just the wrong output. You only catch it by predicting what should happen and comparing.”



Program A stops before running anything. Which line does the message point to? Which quotation mark ended the string too early?
Fix Program A two ways: with double quotation marks around the string, and with \'.
Program B doesn’t crash, but the output is wrong. What did \t and \n do to the folder name? How could you print a backslash? (Try \\.)

title: Lesson 3: Getting Output Right
text:
Teacher Notes

Why a real tool first. Students’ Lesson 2 reports already work. Showing systeminfo (or the macOS and Linux equivalents) gives them a professional standard to aim at, and makes the point that polished output is just careful print() calls. Some school computers block the terminal; if so, show the sample output above.
Tabs aren’t a layout tool. \t jumps to the next multiple of 8 characters, so labels longer than 7 characters jump further and break the line-up. Students meet this on purpose in Investigate. Lesson 4’s f-strings fix it properly (f"{label:<16}{value}").
Windows paths. Program B is a real bug: "C:\temp\new" contains a tab and a new line. It matters in Lesson 6, when students work with paths. Fixes: \\, forward slashes (Windows accepts them in Python), or raw strings (r"C:\temp\new", a later extension).
Commas vs. +. Keep it to text today. "Cores: " + 8 gives a TypeError, which belongs with Lesson 5’s types.
The banner’s right side. The computer’s name is a different length on every computer, so students can’t put it inside a box with a fixed right edge yet. The Quick Build boxes only the title and puts the facts underneath. Lesson 4 comes back to the banner and puts the values inside.
Syntax errors in the step-through box. The box reports the error and highlights the line before anything runs, just as Thonny, IDLE, and VS Code refuse to start the program. Python 3.10 and later say unterminated string literal; older versions say EOL while scanning string literal.
Slides. Open the slides on the projector and this plan on your own screen. Press S for speaker view.
Spiral. Students used print() with commas in Lessons 1–2 without knowing about sep. Keyword arguments come back with round(), sorted(), and open() in later modules.

title: Quick Build: System Banner
text:
Your Program Must

Start with a comment giving your name, the date, and what the program does.
Print a box around a title, drawn with characters such as +, -, =, |, or *. The box has at least three lines, and every line of the box is exactly the same width.

title: Module 3: Benchmark Lab
text:
Planned module. This page shows the direction for Module 3. Lessons, slides, and practice pages are not written yet.
The big idea: students find out how fast the computer really is. A benchmark is just a loop with a stopwatch around it, so this is where loops become the main event: counting, adding, building strings, testing primes, and repeating until time runs out. Students run the same benchmark on the classroom computer, in the browser, and on Google Colab, and explain the difference. They also test themselves against the computer with a reaction timer and a typing test.
Why students care: students compare phones, laptops, and gaming PCs all the time. Here they build the tool that settles the argument, and learn why “faster” depends on what you measure.
Expectations: A2.2, A2.3, A3.1, A3.2, A4.1, A4.4, B1.1, B2.1, B2.4, B3.2, B4.5, C1.2, C1.4

title: Module 3: Benchmark Lab
text:
Anchor Programs

Count to a million: time.perf_counter() around a for loop.
Benchmark suite: several short tests (counting, building a long string, checking for primes), so “fast” is measured more than one way. (Determination of primes, B3.2.)
Reaction timer: wait a random time, say “GO!”, and measure how fast the user presses Enter.
Is shuffle really random? Shuffle a playlist 1000 times and count how often each song plays first, to answer the common complaint that shuffle “keeps playing the same songs”.
Typing speed test: words per minute and accuracy.

title: Module 5: On the Network
text:
Planned module. This page shows the direction for Module 5. Lessons, slides, and practice pages are not written yet.
The big idea: students find out how their computer talks to the rest of the world. Their programs report the computer’s name and address on the network, look up websites, time how long servers take to answer, and download a page to measure the connection. An IP address is a string to split into a list, so this is where lists are written for the first time. Network failures make a natural reason to handle exceptions, and a test log gives students their first reason to write a file.
Why students care: “Is it me or the Wi-Fi?” Students build a troubleshooting tool they can actually use at home, and learn what really happens between typing a web address and seeing the page.
Expectations: A1.2, A1.5, A1.6, A2.3, A3.1, A3.2, A4.5, B1.1, B2.4, B3.3, D2.1

Website lookup: turns a list of web addresses into IP addresses (DNS).
Response timer: times a connection to each server in a list, then reports the fastest, slowest, and average.
Download speed test: downloads a page with urllib and reports the speed in megabits per second.

title: Module 5: On the Network
text:
Notes for Teachers

Open computers needed. On a managed computer, this module is the one most likely to hit the network rules: school proxies and firewalls often block Python’s own connections even when the browser works, and running a server (Lesson 8) is usually forbidden. Check the requirements table with IT before the module starts.
Local only. This module’s programs need a real computer on a real network. The site’s browser boxes can’t open network connections, which makes a good callback to Module 1’s “where does my code run?”
Check with IT first. Some school networks block outside connections, DNS lookups, or student-run servers. Lesson 8 can run on one computer (localhost) if the network won’t allow more.
No ping command needed. Timing a connection with socket.create_connection() works without administrator rights. Students can still read how ping works.
netsim: the public site slows down when a whole class registers at once, which is itself a lesson about server load. A school can host its own copy (source, MIT licence).
Be a good network citizen: small, slow loops only; no scanning other computers.

Planned module. This page shows the direction for Module 7. Lessons, slides, and practice pages are not written yet.
The big idea: students plan, build, test, and present a useful program for a real person. The module starts with a short teacher-led class project, so everyone practises the software development life cycle together, then moves to individual or pair projects.
Why students care: they finish the course with a tool someone actually uses: a family member, a teacher, a club, or themselves.
Expectations: A4.2, A4.5, B1.2, B2.1, B2.2, B2.3, B2.4, B2.5, B4.1, B4.2, B4.3, B4.4, B4.5, B4.6, C3.2

title: Module 7: Software Development Project
section: Part 1: Class Project, “Lab Health Check” (about 4 hours)
text:
Part 1: Class Project, “Lab Health Check” (about 4 hours)
The whole class builds one tool together from the parts of everyone’s My Computer Toolkit. Each team owns one module: system facts (Modules 1–2), a quick benchmark (Module 3), network checks (Module 5), and storage and backups (Module 6). The teacher leads the life cycle out loud.







Lesson
Focus




1. The Software Development Life Cycle
Phases, milestones, and products (B4.1); the class project’s specification


2. Planning Together
A Gantt chart and milestones for the class project (B4.3); dividing the work; a shared skeleton (B2.1)


3. Build, Combine, Test
Teams write their modules; the class combines and tests them (B1.2, B2.3, B4.4)

title: Module 7: Software Development Project
text:
Part 2: Your Own Project (about 12 hours)







Lesson
Focus




4. Find a Real User
Interviews and questionnaires to clarify a specification (B4.2)


5. Design
Structure chart or flow chart (B2.4); user interface: prompts and messages (B2.5); describing the design to a partner (B2.2)


6. Test Plan First
Write the test plan before the code (B4.4, A4.5)


7–9. Work periods
Using documentation independently (C3.2); debugging (B4.5); professional conventions (A4.2); a written status report each period (B4.6)


10. Test and Fix
Run the test plan; record results; fix bugs


11. Present
A short demonstration to the class and, if possible, to the real user

title: Module 7: Software Development Project
text:
Project Ideas
All projects are practical and grow out of the course:

Downloads organizer: sorts files into folders by type, with a dry-run mode that shows what it would do first.
Laptop chooser: asks what a buyer needs and recommends specifications, explaining each choice.
Home network checker: a friendlier version of the Module 5 tool, for a family member.
Family backup tool: backs up chosen folders on a schedule, with a log.
Lab inventory: records the computers in a room and their specifications, and flags the ones due for replacement.
Typing tutor: lessons that get harder, with a progress record.
Energy tracker: a family’s devices, their power use, and what changing habits would save.
Computer parts quiz: quizzes a younger student on hardware vocabulary, with explanations.
Photo organizer: sorts photos into folders by date and reports their sizes (extension: dimensions and thumbnails with the Pillow library).
Toolkit 2.0: a menu-driven version of the student’s own toolkit, for a family member.
A student’s own idea, approved by the teacher.
